title: Mirabel and the Kitchen
premise: Hazel Montrose has spent eleven years tending her late grandfather's lighthouse on the Cornish coast and burying the memory of Theo, the sailor who vanished the night she never gave him her letter. When a storm washes a crate ashore containing that very letter—undelivered, postmarked the day he disappeared—Hazel learns Theo survived and has been searching for her ever since. As she follows the letter's trail to a coastal town where Theo now runs a failing railway café, Hazel must choose between the safe invisibility of her old life and a love that demands she finally be seen. In the end, she stays past the last train, gives him the truth of why she let him go, and they rebuild the café—and each other—together as the lighthouse beam sweeps home.
about_author: Bram Montrose is the pen name of a former railway stationmaster who spent thirty years watching strangers say goodbye on cold platforms. Now writing from a cottage near the sea, Montrose crafts romances about people who almost missed their moment.

chapters.title: The Weight of Water
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. After a violent storm, Hazel walks the tideline and finds a waterlogged crate bearing her grandfather's old lighthouse markings. Inside: a letter in her own handwriting, postmarked eleven years ago—the one she wrote to Theo and never sent. Emotional beat: dread and disbelief; the past knocking at a door she sealed shut.

chapters.title: What the Tide Returned
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, with a flashback to the night Theo left. She rereads the letter and remembers the argument on the platform, the train she watched carry him away without her confession. Her grandmother's voice on the phone urges her to burn it. Emotional beat: guilt resurfacing; loyalty to her grandfather's memory versus the truth she owes herself.

chapters.title: Postmark
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The postmark reveals a town forty miles down the coast—meaning the letter traveled, meaning someone carried it. She researches and finds a listing for 'Theo's Kitchen,' a railway café run by a man with his name. Emotional beat: hope arriving like an intruder; fear that he moved on, or worse, that he didn't.

chapters.title: The Last Train Out
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She takes the coastal line to the town, rehearsing speeches she'll never deliver, and arrives to find the café shuttered and a notice of closure. A neighbor mentions Theo leaves on the last train Friday—for good, a job up north. Emotional beat: urgency; time is running out again, just as it did before.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo closes the café alone, remembering the girl at the lighthouse who never answered his last letter. He kept the café partly because it faces the sea, partly because leaving felt like admitting she was gone. Emotional beat: quiet grief hardened into routine; he's decided survival means letting go.

chapters.title: Salt and Flour
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Hazel finds Theo restocking the empty café at dawn. Their conversation is all deflection and small talk—flour orders, weather—while everything unsaid presses between them. He doesn't mention the letter; she doesn't reveal she knows he searched. Emotional beat: tenderness laced with cowardice; both protecting old wounds.

chapters.title: The Letter He Never Got
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo discovers Hazel's returned letters in a box his landlady kept—every one addressed to the lighthouse, marked undeliverable after Hazel's grandfather died. He realizes she never knew he wrote. Betrayal curdles into fury: someone kept them apart. Emotional beat: rage and revelation; the enemy was silence, not absence.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Lighthouse
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Theo takes the last train to Hazel's village and confronts her in the lantern room. Old accusations fly—she stayed invisible by choice, he left by necessity—and Hazel finally admits she destroyed his letters out of self-protection after grief made her cruel. Emotional beat: climax; love and duty collide, and both must choose truth over safety.

chapters.title: Staying Past the Last Train
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Friday night. The last train whistles through the empty station while Hazel stands on the platform, letter in hand, waiting. Theo steps off instead of on. They exchange the words eleven years overdue—her original letter finally given, his answer finally spoken. Emotional beat: surrender; choosing presence over the safety of departure.

chapters.title: Mirabel and the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, epilogue. Six months later: the café reopens as 'Mirabel'—the name of Theo's boat, and the middle name Hazel's grandmother left her. Hazel writes again, this time about love in the present tense, while the lighthouse beam sweeps over the harbor each night. Emotional beat: resolution; survival redefined not as enduring alone, but as staying.
